title: Practice: Trends in the Periodic Table

questions.stem: Atomic radius decreases across Period 3 from sodium to chlorine. A student claims this is because the atoms have fewer electrons. Why is the student wrong?

options.text: Atoms actually get larger across a period
The number of electrons increases across the period, but so does the nuclear charge, pulling electrons closer to the nucleus
The atoms have the same number of electrons across a period
The electron shells get further from the nucleus across a period

questions.explanation: Across Period 3, each successive element has one more proton and one more electron. However, the extra electrons go into the same shell (the third shell), while the increased nuclear charge (more protons) pulls all the electrons closer to the nucleus. The shielding stays roughly the same, so the effective nuclear attraction increases, shrinking the atom.

questions.stem: Elements change from metals to non-metals across a period. In Period 3, sodium and magnesium are metals, silicon is a metalloid, and phosphorus, sulfur, chlorine, and argon are non-metals. How does this relate to their oxides?

options.text: All Period 3 oxides are acidic
Metal oxides on the left are basic, while non-metal oxides on the right are acidic
All Period 3 oxides are basic
Non-metal oxides on the right are basic, while metal oxides on the left are acidic

questions.explanation: There is a clear trend across Period 3: metal oxides (e.g., Na₂O, MgO) are basic — they react with acids. Non-metal oxides (e.g., SO₃, P₄O₁₀) are acidic — they react with bases. Aluminium oxide is amphoteric (reacts with both acids and bases), sitting at the transition point.

questions.stem: Going down Group 1, reactivity increases, but going down Group 7, reactivity decreases. What is the underlying reason for this opposite trend?

options.text: Group 1 metals gain electrons while Group 7 non-metals lose electrons
Group 1 metals lose electrons (easier with more shells), while Group 7 non-metals gain electrons (harder with more shells and shielding)
Group 1 elements get smaller going down, while Group 7 elements get larger
There is no underlying reason; it is just a coincidence

questions.explanation: Group 1 metals react by losing their outer electron. More shells mean greater distance and shielding, making it easier to lose the electron — so reactivity increases down the group. Group 7 non-metals react by gaining an electron. More shells and shielding reduce the attraction for an incoming electron — so reactivity decreases down the group.

questions.stem: Melting points across Period 3 rise from sodium to silicon, then drop sharply for phosphorus, sulfur, chlorine, and argon. What explains the sharp drop?

options.text: Phosphorus, sulfur, chlorine, and argon are non-metals with simple molecular or atomic structures held by weak intermolecular forces
These elements have fewer protons so their bonds are weaker
These elements are all gases at room temperature
These elements have metallic bonding that becomes weaker

questions.explanation: Na, Mg, and Al are metals with strong metallic bonding. Silicon has a giant covalent structure with very strong bonds. But P₄, S₈, Cl₂, and Ar are simple molecules or atoms. The forces between these molecules (intermolecular forces) are much weaker than metallic or covalent network bonds, so much less energy is needed to separate them.

questions.stem: First ionisation energy generally increases across a period but decreases down a group. Which element would have the lowest first ionisation energy?

options.text: Helium (top right of the table)
Fluorine (top of Group 7)
Caesium (bottom of Group 1)
Carbon (middle of Period 2)

questions.explanation: First ionisation energy is lowest for elements at the bottom-left of the periodic table. Caesium (bottom of Group 1) has the most electron shells and the most shielding, with only 1 outer electron that is very far from the nucleus. This makes it the easiest electron to remove, giving the lowest ionisation energy among the options.
